Currently a plate meal is $5.50 it comes with your choice of meat, 3 sides, and cornbread/roll. There is something for everyone. You can even get a veggie plate. My favorite is the baked chicken. It's delicious and seasoned to perfection. All fried items are cooked when ordered.

The best part about eating lunch here is knowing that my purchase is going towards the Ministry of Lizzies House. It's a shelter for Women & Children.

That’s how we ended up at a place I’d somehow never heard of.

And honestly, that’s usually a good sign.

Enter The Walk-In.

The place has this interesting mix going on. It feels Southern when you walk in - relaxed, comfortable, a little quirky - but the food leans Asian in ways that make the menu fun to poke around.

So we what we usually do when we’re somewhere new. We ordered a handful of things and figured we’d sort it out when it hit the table.

The black garlic deviled eggs were the first thing out. Just two halves, but really interesting. Salty in a good way with soy sauce, bonito, green onions, and sesame. Familiar, but not something you see every day.

The crab rangoon was excellent. Crispy and hot with a mango sweet and sour sauce that worked really well.

The kung pao bao buns were great too. Crispy chicken, crushed peanuts, soft buns. Good stuff.

We also tried the bulgogi grilled cheese, which comes as four little pull-apart Hawaiian roll sliders with beef tenderloin, kimchi, and mozzarella. Sweet rolls, savory beef, a little tang from the kimchi. A fun combination.

And because I’m me, we added the burger too. Patty melt style with house chips. Cooked perfectly.

Somewhere in the middle of all that I realized I was eating tater tots with chopsticks. Which felt like a pretty good summary of the whole experience.

They’ve got a patio outside and a shelf full of board games. I spotted Sorry and that was the end of that.

And I’m proud to report I ended the night with a victory.

Super fun little place. Quiet. Quirky. The kind of spot you’re happy you stumble into.

Some nights you just get The kung pao bao buns were great too. Crispy chicken, crushed peanuts, soft buns. Good stuff.

And because I’m me, we added the burger too. Patty melt style with house chips. Cooked perfectly.

Somewhere in the middle of all that I realized I was eating tater tots with chopsticks. Which felt like a pretty good summary of the whole experience.

They’ve got a patio outside and a shelf full of board games. I spotted Sorry and that was the end of that.

And I’m proud to report I ended the night with a victory.

We began with a play of contrasts and texture: hand-cut beef tartare elevated by chive and dill, crowned with a whisper of smoked salt and served alongside golden-grilled bread. Beside it, Oysters Elvaretta — kissed with bacon, Parmesan, and tender artichoke — offering a briny depth softened by a crisp French baguette.
The main courses arrived in a duet of indulgence. First, “Pork Two Ways” — confit pork belly yielding beneath its crackling skin, paired with crisp rillettes, confit Alabama apples, silky miso butternut squash, and bright pickled mustard seeds that illuminated each bite. Then, Mississippi braised beef cheek, rich and unctuous, glazed in Hoover sauce and served with local carrots, a French onion soubise, and a touch of horseradish and toasted benne seeds — a dish that spoke of patience, craft, and the quiet power of Southern terroir.
Dessert brought a final note of comfort and grace. A salted caramel and chocolate brownie — molten within — paired with vanilla ice cream, benne seed crumble, and sea salt. Beside it, an espresso layered pudding with mascarpone, crisp wafers, and praline dulce de leche, each spoonful an embrace of brightness and depth.

Drago’s originated in Louisiana and has expanded into neighboring states, and this stop genuinely felt like our stomach arrived in New Orleans before we did. It was a great introduction to Southern and Cajun-style seafood before reaching NOLA.

The restaurant has a classic American bar-meets–fine dining atmosphere. The dining room is spacious and brightly lit with chandeliers, and the walls are decorated with framed New Orleans street scenes, giving the space a subtle sense of “exported” NOLA culture. There is also a full bar area, where TVs were playing live sports, making it a comfortable spot for both dining and casually watching a game. On a weekday evening, the restaurant wasn’t crowded, which made the experience relaxed and unhurried—perfect after a long drive.

Reservations are available, which is nice to know if you’re stopping by during busier hours or on weekends. The menu itself is not very large, but it’s focused. If you’re particular about choices, it’s worth checking the menu online in advance so you know what to expect.

The highlight of the meal was Drago’s Original Charbroiled Oysters. They arrived sizzling at the table, filled with rich garlic butter aroma and sound. Paired with hand-torn bread for soaking up the sauce, they were absolutely addictive and disappeared almost instantly. This dish alone is reason enough to visit.
We also ordered the Fried Gator Bites, made from battered and fried alligator tail meat served with remoulade sauce. They’re surprisingly approachable—think “chicken nuggets,” but firmer and more substantial than chicken, with a satisfying bite.
The Mama Ruth’s Seafood Gumbo was thick, rich, and hearty, with a strong seafood-and-okra base. It works especially well mixed with rice, making it a comforting and filling dish.
Fish, Shrimp ’N’ Grits was another standout. The grits were creamy and fragrant, topped with fish and shrimp, and packed with flavor. Unexpectedly, it even reminded us of Chinese “fish-fragrant” flavors in a fun way.

After hours on the road, this meal completely washed away our travel fatigue. With multiple locations in New Orleans, Drago’s feels like a dependable choice with consistent quality. Whether you’re passing through Mississippi or dining in NOLA, it’s a solid stop for satisfying Southern seafood in a comfortable, no-rush I’m a 25 plus year cigar smoker and when I travel anywhere, I look for a cigar lounge to checkout. Before I left home in Milwaukee a friend gave me 2 recommendations, I checked out the first website and didn’t have to checkout the second. I was impressed by the website and decided to call to inform them that I was coming. Selma answered the phone and by her conversation and warmness over the phone I knew I most likely had found my new cigar lounge I’d be attending on my visits to Mississippi. I was still hoping the in person experience would match the phone experience.

When I arrived it was clear I had chose the right lounge! I pull up to a beautiful, massive, late 1800’s home with plenty free, on promise parking. I make my way inside where I was greeted by 2 young ladies which ended up being server/bartenders. After a brief conversation about the house, I followed one of the ladies recommendation on a house cigar, which turned out to be a great selection and got my Macallan 12 neat. She asked if I wanted a tour of the house/lounge, of course I did! I am a sucker for a vintage establishment and this place was everything! It’s very well maintained and the decor just adds to the atmosphere.

After the tour I was welcomed to sit in a lounge area with 3 individuals, after not long finding out 2 of them was Selma (co-owner) and Terris (co-owner). After 2 cigars, 2 glasses of Macallan and almost 3 hours of great conversation, I’m pleased to let you know I have a new cigar lounge that I will be attending EVERY TIME I visit my son at JSU and I’m sure even when I’m not visiting my son 😂.

Thank you Terris and Selma for the great time last night! Y’all made this very emotional and financially draining trip to Mississippi to drop my son off so much better!!! Lol

Until next time,
